artiest/esa-pekka-salonen.text:
Esa-Pekka Salonen is a Finnish conductor and composer, born in Helsinki in 1958. He studied horn and composition at the Sibelius Academy and conducting with Jorma Panula. With his fellow student Magnus Lindberg he founded the new-music group Korvat auki and the experimental ensemble Toimii. At first he saw himself mainly as a composer, and began conducting in order to have his own work performed. In 1983 he stepped in at short notice for Michael Tilson Thomas in Mahler's Third Symphony with the Philharmonia Orchestra in London, without knowing the score. That launched his conducting career.

From 1984 to 1995 he was chief conductor of the Swedish Radio Symphony Orchestra, and from 1985 to 1994 principal guest conductor of the Philharmonia. In 1984 he made his debut in the United States with the Los Angeles Philharmonic, of which he later became music director. From 2020 to 2025 he led the San Francisco Symphony. In 2003, with Michael Tydén and Valery Gergiev, he founded the Baltic Sea Festival. His recordings begin in 1986, with Messiaen's Turangalîla-Symphonie, Sibelius and Stravinsky, including The Firebird and Le Sacre du Printemps.

Salonen brings the classical tradition and new music together. He conducts Sibelius and Stravinsky, but also Lutosławski, Messiaen and his own work. In this way he is one of the conductors who gave contemporary music a permanent place in the great orchestral repertoire.
artiest/esa-pekka-salonen.listen: Listen to his recording of Le Sacre du Printemps and notice how clearly the sharp rhythms and the clashing chords are played, with a transparent orchestral sound.

artiest/esbjorn-svensson.text: The pianist Esbjörn Svensson grew up in Västerås in Sweden. With his boyhood friend, the drummer Magnus Öström, and the bassist Dan Berglund he founded the Esbjörn Svensson Trio in 1993. He named Keith Jarrett and classical music as important influences. The trio played quiet ballads and loud pieces with effects, such as a distorted bass and electronics, and performed in rock venues. In 2006 e.s.t. became the first European jazz group on the cover of DownBeat. In June 2008 Svensson died in a diving accident near Stockholm.
artiest/esbjorn-svensson.listen: Hear how the bass with effects sounds like an electric guitar.

artiest/esbjorn-svensson-trio.text:
The Esbjörn Svensson Trio, e.s.t. for short, was a Swedish jazz piano trio formed in 1993 by the pianist Esbjörn Svensson, the bassist Dan Berglund and the drummer Magnus Öström. The trio deliberately blurred the boundaries between genres. Svensson drew his influences from widely varying music, and the band named the classical composer Béla Bartók and the rock band Radiohead as inspirations. In the music one can hear elements of classical, rock, pop and techno, alongside ordinary jazz and the use of electronic effects and multitrack recording.

The trio was known for its lively performances, often in rock clubs for a young audience, and had great success and acclaim throughout Europe. In 1995 and 1996 Svensson was named Swedish jazz musician of the year, and the album Winter in Venice from 1997 won the Swedish Grammy. The album From Gagarin's Point of View from 1999 marked the beginning of their international breakthrough. The album Strange Place For Snow from 2002 won many awards, including the German Jahrespreis der Deutschen Schallplattenkritik and the French Victoire du Jazz for best international act.

On 14 June 2008 Svensson died in a diving accident in Stockholm. Since 2013 Öström and Berglund have toured with the project e.s.t. symphony, with the arranger Hans Ek, in which the songs are played in symphonic versions. The trio showed that a jazz piano trio could also sound like a rock band and that young listeners would come for it.
artiest/esbjorn-svensson-trio.listen: Listen to From Gagarin's Point of View and notice the interplay between piano, bass and drums. Where does it sound like jazz, and where more like rock or electronic music?

artiest/esperanza-spalding.text: Esperanza Spalding, from Portland, Oregon, played violin as a child and later chose the double bass. She studied at Berklee, where she was already teaching at the age of twenty. She sings and plays bass at the same time, often in complex rhythms and in English, Spanish and Portuguese. In 2011 she won the Grammy for best new artist, the first jazz musician to do so. Her albums range from chamber music with strings to funk and rock. She worked with Wayne Shorter on the opera Iphigenia. She teaches at Harvard.
artiest/esperanza-spalding.listen: Notice how she sings and plays a different line on the bass at the same time.

artiest/esso-trinidad-steel-band.text:
The Esso Trinidad Steel Band was a steel band from Trinidad that existed from 1942 to 1976. The group began in 1942 as the Tripoli Steel Band, named after a line in the hymn of the US Marines. In 1951 Hugh Borde took over as leader. He improved the band's technique and made it a serious contender in the Carnival competitions. In 1964 the group won the Steel Band Music Festival.

In 1965 the oil company Esso began to sponsor the group, after which it changed its name. With that support the band grew to twenty-eight members, acquired uniforms and new instruments, and in 1967 played at Expo 67 in Montreal. That led to a record contract with ARC Sound in Toronto and then with Warner Bros. Records. Van Dyke Parks produced a full album that was released in 1971, titled Esso. It was nominated for a Grammy in the category of ethnic or traditional recording, but lost to Muddy Waters. Calypso Christmas had already appeared earlier, in 1967.

Shortly after the album Esso withdrew its sponsorship. The group called itself the Trinidad Tripoli Steel Band and toured internationally with Liberace. Parks called them the best group he had ever had the chance to produce. In 1976 Borde moved with his family to Ypsilanti, Michigan, and the Trinidadian group came to an end. His sons continued under the name Trinidad Tripoli Steel Band. The band let North American audiences hear how rich and sophisticated steel band music could sound.
artiest/esso-trinidad-steel-band.listen: Listen to a track from the 1971 album Esso and notice the bright, metallic sound of the steel pans, with the melody passing back and forth between different pans.

artiest/ethan-iverson.text:
Ethan Iverson is an American pianist, composer and music critic, born in Menomonie, Wisconsin, in 1973. He studied with Fred Hersch and Sophia Rosoff and was musical director of the Mark Morris Dance Group before forming the avant-garde jazz trio The Bad Plus with the bassist Reid Anderson and the drummer Dave King. In 2017 he left the group and was succeeded by Orrin Evans. He is affiliated with the New England Conservatory.

After The Bad Plus his work moved in more directions. In 2017 he wrote Pepperland for the Mark Morris Dance Group, a score based on parts of Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band by the Beatles, and led the band at the performances. In 2018 Temporary Kings appeared on ECM with the saxophonist Mark Turner, and in 2019 Common Practice with the trumpeter Tom Harrell, recorded at the Village Vanguard. In 2022 came his first record for Blue Note, Every Note Is True, with Larry Grenadier and Jack DeJohnette. In 2024 Technically Acceptable and Playfair Sonatas followed. He also played with Billy Hart, Lee Konitz, Paul Motian, Charlie Haden and Ron Carter.

Iverson also writes about music for, among others, The New Yorker and NPR, and publishes on his own Substack. He shows how a contemporary jazz musician knows the tradition of the piano trio and also plays with it, for example by turning popular music by the Beatles into dance music and by writing critically about jazz history.
artiest/ethan-iverson.listen: Listen to a track from Every Note Is True and notice how pianist, bassist and drummer follow each other as equals and together keep the trio's rhythm open.

artiest/ethel-waters.text:
Ethel Waters was born in Chester, Pennsylvania, in 1896 and grew up in poverty with her grandmother, who worked as a domestic servant. She never lived in the same place for longer than fifteen months. At thirteen she married for the first time, but her husband was violent and she soon left him. She worked as a chambermaid in a hotel in Philadelphia for 4.75 dollars a week, until on her seventeenth birthday she went to a costume party in a nightclub and performed there.

In the 1920s she began as a blues singer. She sang jazz, swing and pop on the stage of Broadway and in concert halls. Her well-known recordings include Dinah, Taking a Chance on Love, Heat Wave, Supper Time, Am I Blue? and Cabin in the Sky. Stormy Weather from 1933 is one of her greatest songs. She was also an actress, on stage and in film.

Waters sang with a clear, precise diction and could join blues and cabaret seamlessly. Her delivery, in which every word counts, shows how Black women singers in the 1920s and 1930s raised the popular song to a higher level. She died in 1977.
artiest/ethel-waters.listen: Listen to Stormy Weather and notice how Waters almost tells the lyrics, with long, calm phrases and little ornamentation. What feelings do you hear in her voice?

artiest/etienne-de-crecy.text:
Étienne de Crécy is a French DJ and producer of electronic music, above all house. He was born in Lyon in 1969 and moved from Marseille to Versailles in the mid-1980s. There he attended the same school as the members of Air and Alex Gopher, with whom he later founded the label Solid. As a sound engineer in a Parisian studio he met Philippe Zdar of Cassius. Together they made the album Pansoul as Motorbass. He also produced under names such as Superdiscount and Mooloodjee.

His first solo album was Super Discount, from 1997, with the singles Tout doit disparaître and Prix Choc. Together with Air, Alex Gopher and other French artists on Solid, it was a cornerstone of the French house wave. Four years later came Tempovision, which he himself called a blues album. It includes Am I Wrong, with a sample of Millie Jackson, which reached the British chart in January 2001. The three animated 3D videos for the singles were made by his brother Geoffroy de Crécy. In 2004 Super Discount 2 followed, for which he used only old analogue instruments, such as a TB-303. All the tracks are named after a peer-to-peer program, such as Overnet and Limewire. Super Discount 3 appeared in 2015, B.E.D in 2018 and Warm Up in 2025.

De Crécy belongs to the French electronic music of the 1990s, the French touch. He combines danceable filtered house with sampling, humour and a concern for the shape of the album. His work shows that club music can be more than just separate singles.
artiest/etienne-de-crecy.listen: Listen to Am I Wrong from Tempovision and notice how the sampled soul voice is repeated and turned into a dance track by the electronic rhythms and bass.

artiest/etta-james.text:
Etta James's real name was Jamesetta Hawkins and she was born in Los Angeles in 1938. Her mother was only fourteen, and Etta grew up with foster parents and relatives. At the age of five she received singing lessons from the choirmaster of a Baptist church, and soon she was singing solo in the choir. In San Francisco, as a teenager, she started a girl group, The Creolettes. The musician Johnny Otis took the group under his wing and reversed her first name to make Etta James.

In 1955 her song The Wallflower reached number 1 on the R&B chart. In 1960 she signed with Chess Records, where she became one of the first stars. Leonard Chess saw a ballad singer in her and surrounded her with violins. That is how At Last (1960), her best-known song, came about. Among the songs that followed were Something's Got a Hold on Me (1962), Tell Mama and I'd Rather Go Blind (1967). For a long time she suffered from a heroin addiction and other problems, but made a comeback in the late 1980s with Seven Year Itch (1988). For Mystery Lady, songs by Billie Holiday, she won a Grammy.

Etta James had a deep, earthy voice that felt at home in gospel, blues, jazz, R&B, rock 'n' roll and soul. She is seen as a bridge between R&B and rock 'n' roll. In 1993 she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Her voice also lives on in new music: Avicii used a sample from Something's Got a Hold on Me for his hit Levels. She died in 2012.
artiest/etta-james.listen: First listen to Something's Got a Hold on Me by Etta James and then to Levels by Avicii. Notice how her powerful soul voice from 1962 turns up in the dance track, as a short fragment among the electronic sounds.

artiest/eubie-blake.text:
James Hubert Blake, better known as Eubie Blake, was an American pianist and composer of ragtime, jazz and popular music. He was born in Baltimore in 1887, the only one of his parents' children to survive childhood. Both his parents had been born into slavery. He later said that he was born in 1883, but census documents and his passport point to 1887. At the age of four or five he began playing an organ in a music shop, and at seven he was taught by an organist. At fifteen he played piano in a Baltimore brothel, and from 1907 at the Goldfield Hotel, a club owned by the boxing champion Joe Gans.

His career began in 1912. After the First World War he worked with the singer Noble Sissle. Together they wrote Shuffle Along in 1921, one of the first Broadway musicals written and directed by African Americans. His best-known compositions include Charleston Rag, Bandana Days, Love Will Find a Way, Memories of You and I'm Just Wild About Harry. After the Second World War he worked with Sissle at the USO. In 1978 the musical Eubie! showcased his work, and in 1981 he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Ronald Reagan.

Blake linked the ragtime of the turn of the century with the musical theatre of Broadway. You can hear his fast, rhythmically layered piano playing on records such as Golden Reunion In Ragtime and Rags To Classics. He died in 1983, five days after his ninety-sixth birthday.
artiest/eubie-blake.listen: Listen to Charleston Rag in Blake's own recording and notice how the left hand plays a firm rhythm while the right hand dances over it with fast, displaced notes.

artiest/eugene-wright.text:
Eugene Wright was an American jazz bassist, born in Chicago in 1923. In high school he played cornet and in his twenties he led the sixteen-piece band the Dukes of Swing. On bass he was largely self-taught, until in his early thirties he took private lessons. His idol was Walter Page. He played with Count Basie, Erroll Garner, Billie Holiday and Charlie Parker, with bebop musicians such as Sonny Stitt and, in Latin jazz, with Cal Tjader. From 1952 to 1955 he worked with Buddy DeFranco, and in 1955 in the trio of Red Norvo.

His best-known engagement began in 1958, when he joined the Dave Brubeck Quartet. Until 1968 he was part of the classic line-up with Paul Desmond and Joe Morello. He played on the standards Take Five and Blue Rondo à la Turk and recorded more than thirty albums with the group. Brubeck wrote that Wright's steady bass anchored the group, so that the others could play other time signatures and polyrhythms. In 1962 he sang and played in the jazz musical The Real Ambassadors, with vocals by Louis Armstrong and Carmen McRae.

Wright also became known for what he experienced. Some concert promoters did not want a Black musician next to the three white members, but Brubeck refused to perform without him. In 1960 Brubeck cancelled a tour of twenty-five universities in the South, because twenty-two schools would not admit Wright. Among jazz musicians he was known as The Senator. After his years with Brubeck he played from 1971 to 1974 in the trio of Monty Alexander. He died in 2020.
artiest/eugene-wright.listen: Listen to Take Five by the Dave Brubeck Quartet and notice the steady, calm bass figure in 5/4 time over which piano and saxophone play.

artiest/eureka-brass-band.text:
The Eureka Brass Band was a brass band from New Orleans that was active from 1920 to 1975. The trumpeter Willie Wilson founded the group. Its early members included the clarinettists Willie Parker, John Casimir and George Lewis and the cornettist Kid Rena. The line-up varied, usually from nine to eleven musicians, and generally consisted of three trumpets, two trombones, two reeds, a tuba, a snare drum and a bass drum. In the 1930s Wilson fell ill, and after 1937 the sousaphonist Joseph Red Clark briefly took over. Dominique T-Boy Remy followed, and later Percy Humphrey.

The band recorded extensively for, among others, Atlantic Records, Pax, Alamac, Folkways, Jazzology and Sounds of New Orleans. The album New Orleans Parade from 1951 features Humphrey with trombonists Charles Sunny Henry and Albert Warner, among others, and in 1962 the album Jazz at Preservation Hall, Vol. 1 appeared on Atlantic, with Humphrey, his brother, the clarinettist Willie Humphrey, and the trumpeters Kid Sheik Cola and Pete Bocage. Although the group broke up after 1975, Humphrey sometimes revived the name for festivals and other appearances.

The Eureka Brass Band played the tradition of the New Orleans street band, which made music for parades and funerals. Such bands were a source of early jazz, and this group kept that old way of playing alive for decades, with several melodic lines at once above a solid march rhythm.
artiest/eureka-brass-band.listen: Listen to Just a Little While to Stay Here and notice how the brass play one song together and how the snare drum and bass drum provide the march rhythm. Can you also hear individual voices playing in between?

artiest/europa-galante.text:
Europa Galante is an Italian Baroque orchestra on period instruments, founded in 1990 by the violinist Fabio Biondi, who also leads it. The group began its career with a recording of Vivaldi's Le quattro stagioni (The Four Seasons) in 1991. Vivaldi concertos followed, Corelli's concerti grossi, Salve Regina and chamber music by Boccherini, including six trios op. 47 and string quintets.

The repertoire is broad. It includes operas by Cavalli, oratorios by Caldara, oratorios and concertos by Scarlatti, and recently also Bellini's Norma and Donizetti's Anna Bolena. The ensemble first recorded for the French label Opus 111, then for ten years for Virgin Classics, where Vivaldi's La stravaganza, Scarlatti's Concerti e Sinfonie and the operas Bajazet and Ercole su'l Termodonte were released. Later it also recorded for the Spanish Glossa, including Il diario di Chiara with music from the Pietà in Venice and, in 2014, Vivaldi's Farewell Concertos. In 1997 the group was nominated for a Grammy for best small ensemble. It has played at La Scala, the Concertgebouw, the Royal Albert Hall, Lincoln Center and the Sydney Opera House, with soloists such as Roberta Invernizzi, Ian Bostridge and Philippe Jaroussky.

Europa Galante belongs to the generation that made the performance of Baroque music on period instruments more energetic and direct in the 1990s. Their Four Seasons in particular, with its lively, almost theatrical playing, brought Vivaldi to a wide audience.
artiest/europa-galante.listen: Listen to Spring from Vivaldi's Le quattro stagioni in the recording by Europa Galante and notice how the soloist and the strings depict the birds, the water and the thunderstorm with sharp accents.

artiest/europe.text:
Europe is a Swedish rock band founded in 1979 in Upplands Väsby near Stockholm, at first under the name Force. The first line-up consisted of the singer Joey Tempest, the guitarist John Norum, the bassist Peter Olsson and the drummer Tony Reno. Demo tapes sent to record companies brought the demand that the band cut its hair and sing in Swedish. In 1982 the group became the first to win the television contest Rock-SM, the Swedish rock championship, and that was the breakthrough in its home country. Olsson was succeeded by John Levén.

The first two albums, Europe in 1983 and Wings of Tomorrow in 1984, did reasonably well only in Sweden. The international breakthrough came with the third album, The Final Countdown, in 1986. The title song reached number eight in the American Hot 100 and Carrie number three, and Rock the Night reached number thirty. Out of This World followed in 1988 and Prisoners in Paradise in 1991. In 1992 the band went on indefinite hiatus, but in 1999 it came together again for a performance on New Year's Eve in Stockholm. In 2003 an official reunion followed, with albums such as Start from the Dark, Secret Society, War of Kings and Walk the Earth, and in 2026 Come This Madness.

The music is melodic hard rock with a striking synthesizer riff, sung with a clear, powerful voice. That made Europe the best-known Swedish rock band after ABBA in the 1980s. The success showed that rock from Scandinavia could reach the international charts.
artiest/europe.listen: Listen to The Final Countdown and notice the synthesizer riff at the beginning, which keeps coming back, and how the guitar and the vocals drive the song towards the chorus.

artiest/eurythmics.text:
Eurythmics was a British pop duo of the Scottish singer Annie Lennox and the English musician and producer Dave Stewart. The two met in 1975 in a London restaurant where Lennox worked, and at first played together in the bands The Catch and The Tourists. In 1980, in a hotel in Australia, playing on a small synthesizer, they decided to continue as a duo. They wanted to make pop music, but with the freedom to experiment with electronics.

The first album, In the Garden (1981), was recorded in Cologne with the producer Conny Plank and members of Can, but sold poorly. With a bank loan Lennox and Stewart then built their own eight-track studio above a picture framer's in London. There Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) (1983) came into being. The title track, with a dark, programmed synthesizer bass, became a worldwide hit, including in the United States. In the video Lennox appeared with cropped orange hair and a man's suit. Love Is a Stranger, Here Comes the Rain Again and There Must Be an Angel (Playing with My Heart) followed.

Eurythmics showed that two people with a small studio and electronic instruments could make worldwide hits. With her cool voice and her play with male and female roles, Lennox became one of the most striking female singers of the 1980s. In 1990 the duo split up. Lennox began a solo career, and Stewart became a sought-after producer. In 1999 they came together once more for the album Peace.
artiest/eurythmics.listen: Listen to Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) and follow the synthesizer bass, which keeps repeating the same pattern throughout the song. Notice how Annie Lennox's cool voice floats above it.

artiest/eva-simons.text:
Eva Simons is a Dutch singer, songwriter and music video director from Amsterdam. She grew up in a musical family. Her mother, Ingrid Simons, is a backing singer of Surinamese descent, her grandfather was the accordionist Johnny Meijer and her father was a pianist. As a teenager she sang in Jody's Kids, a group that supplied vocals for production music. She graduated from the Conservatorium van Amsterdam. In 2004 she took part in the Dutch Popstars The Rivals and became a member of the group Raffish, which had a hit with Plaything and released the album How Raffish Are You? in 2005. She left the group that summer.

In 2009 a demo of her song Silly Boy leaked on YouTube, with four million viewers. Some thought it was an unreleased single by Lady Gaga or Rihanna. She then signed with EMI. With the songwriting duo Topline Ink she wrote Take Over Control, which DJ Afrojack produced. The song spent six weeks in the American Top Dance Airplay chart and became a dance classic worldwide. In 2011 she signed a major American contract and sang on LMFAO's Best Night. She also worked with will.i.am, and her breakthrough abroad came in 2012 with the single This Is Love. Policeman is her best-known song of her own.

Eva Simons represents the generation of Dutch artists who broke through internationally in the 2010s via the dance scene. She combines pop vocals with the electronic production of DJs, a collaboration that dominated the charts in that period.
artiest/eva-simons.listen: Listen to Take Over Control with Afrojack and notice how the vocals keep building up over a heavy electronic beat towards the drop.

artiest/evan-parker.text: The saxophonist Evan Parker, from Bristol, fell under the spell of John Coltrane as a teenager. In London he played in John Stevens's Spontaneous Music Ensemble and with the guitarist Derek Bailey. In 1970, with Bailey and the drummer Tony Oxley, he founded the label Incus. Parker developed a technique of his own on the soprano saxophone using circular breathing: he breathes in through his nose while continuing to blow, so that he can play for minutes without interruption. This produces layers of rapidly repeated patterns and overtones. He also played for a long time in the trio of Alexander von Schlippenbach, and in 2017 with the young London duo Binker and Moses.
artiest/evan-parker.listen: Listen without counting: can you hear when he breathes?

artiest/ewe-zangers-en-slagwerkers-uit-a.text:
The Ewe are a people in south-eastern Ghana and in the neighbouring countries of Togo and Benin. Anyako lies in the Ghanaian part of that region, in the Volta Region, and is known for its living musical tradition. The singers and drummers from this village are not a band in the Western sense of the word. They are community musicians who sing and drum at festivals, ceremonies and dances, as has been done there for generations.

The piece in the course is a 1972 field recording of Atsiagbekor. This is a dance with a military background, which is also performed in the area around Anyako. The music is based on rhythm: several drums and an iron double bell each play a pattern of their own, and those patterns coincide on a fixed cycle. A lead drummer gives signals to the dancers, and the singing works in call and response, with a lead singer answered by a group.

Ewe music matters for the history of pop because it shows how rhythm in West Africa is built from layers that cross one another. That principle of thought, polyrhythm instead of a single beat, returns later in much music that came out of Africa and the African diaspora. A field recording like this shows the source without studio or processing.
artiest/ewe-zangers-en-slagwerkers-uit-a.listen: Listen to the bell and the drums in Atsiagbekor. First try to follow only the high, constantly recurring bell pattern and then notice how the other rhythms revolve around it.

artiest/ex-libris-ensemble-en-daniil-say.text:
The Ex Libris Ensemble and Daniil Sayapin are the performers of the Troparion of the Holy Trinity in the 2020 version that the course uses. Nothing about the musicians themselves is recorded in the available sources, so this entry is mainly about the tradition from which the piece comes.

The chant belongs to Znamenny chant, the oldest form of Russian Orthodox church music. Znamenny chant is monophonic. There is no accompaniment and no chord changes: the singers follow a single melodic line, sometimes with a drone (bourdon) beneath. The melodies were written down in a notation of their own, made up of signs, the kryuki or znamena, from which the chant takes its name. The tradition arose in the Middle Ages, when Christianity spread across Kievan Rus, and is still sung in the liturgy today.

For anyone learning to listen to pop, Znamenny chant is a useful counterpart. There are no drums, no chorus and no harmony driving the piece forward. Everything depends on the line of the voice and on the text, which in the liturgy is what matters most. Anyone who sets this beside pop music hears how many choices in the modern song are not self-evident.
artiest/ex-libris-ensemble-en-daniil-say.listen: Listen to the Troparion of the Holy Trinity and notice what is missing: no fixed beat, no instruments, no chords. Simply follow how the voices carry the melody.

artiest/extince.text:
Extince, real name Peter Kops, was born in 1967 in Oosterhout, in the province of North Brabant. He is also known as De Exter. In the 1980s he moved to Amsterdam and rapped in English. The Milkshake Rap (1987) became a minor hit, but was withdrawn from sale after a claim from McDonald's over a sample. In 1994, at the request of Def P of the Osdorp Posse, he recorded the Dutch-language Turbotaal. After that he rapped only in Dutch.

Spraakwater (1995), produced by DJ Knowhow, reached number eight in the Top 40. It is regarded as the first Dutch-language hip hop hit in the top 10. The intro opens with the familiar jingle for the number 1 of the Top 40 and a quotation from Meneer de Uil (Mr Owl) in De Fabeltjeskrant. Then comes a relaxed funk beat over which Extince raps smoothly and with a Brabant accent. Not everyone was pleased. Def P found it too commercial and replied with Braakwater, to which Extince responded with Kaal of Kammen. Spraakwater became the first single from his Dutch-language debut album Binnenlandse Funk (1998).

After Vitamine E (2001) came a feud on record with Brainpower. Extince kept making albums, from Toch? (2007) to Kermis (2019), and in 2020 released Spraakwater 25. In 2005 he received a Gouden Greep for his entire career and in 2018 an Edison Oeuvreprijs. What Doe Maar did with ska around 1980, Extince did with hip hop: he turned a foreign style into a hit in his own language, and so paved the way for later Dutch-language rappers.
artiest/extince.listen: Notice the start of Spraakwater: first you hear the jingle with which the Top 40 announces its number 1, then Meneer de Uil from De Fabeltjeskrant. Only then does the funk beat kick in, and you can hear how Extince makes long Dutch words rhyme.

artiest/ezra-collective.text:
Ezra Collective is a British jazz quintet from London. The group came together in 2012 around the brothers Femi Koleoso on drums and TJ Koleoso on bass guitar. They were joined by the keyboard player Joe Armon-Jones, the saxophonist James Mollison and a trumpeter, today Ife Ogunjobi. The members met at Tomorrow's Warriors, a London jazz programme for young people. The name refers to the prophet Ezra, who studied the works of his predecessors, as the band wanted to do with jazz.

The debut album You Can't Steal My Joy appeared in 2019, with Jorja Smith and Loyle Carner among the guests. In 2022 came Where I'm Meant to Be, which won the Mercury Prize in 2023. Ezra Collective were thereby the first jazz act to receive that prize. In 2025 the group also won a Brit Award for best group. Dance, No One's Watching followed in 2024 and Here Because of Hope in 2026.

The music mixes jazz with Afrobeat, calypso, reggae, hip hop and soul. The result is danceable and energetic, and the band emphatically seeks the live effect. Ezra Collective belong to the new London jazz, a scene that brought jazz back to a young audience. Femi Koleoso himself used to see jazz as an elitist art form, and the group wants precisely to break that image.
artiest/ezra-collective.listen: Listen to Victory Dance and follow Femi Koleoso's drums, which drive the whole piece. Notice too how the horns and the keyboards build a festive atmosphere on that rhythmic base.

artiest/fab-morvan.text:
Fabrice Morvan, Fab Morvan for short, is a French singer, dancer, rapper and model, born in Paris in 1966. His parents came from Pointe-à-Pitre in Guadeloupe. At eighteen he moved to Germany, where he worked as a dancer and model and was influenced by funk, soul, hip hop and pop. In a nightclub in Munich he met Rob Pilatus, and together they decided to form a rock and soul group.

The producer Frank Farian discovered them and had them perform as Milli Vanilli. They were the face of the singers Charles Shaw, John Davis and Brad Howell, whom Farian considered talented but who, in his view, lacked a marketable image. The first album, Girl You Know It's True from 1989, was popular worldwide and produced four hits: the title song, Girl I'm Gonna Miss You, Baby Don't Forget My Number and Blame It on the Rain. On 22 February 1990 the group won a Grammy for best new artist. Rumours of lip-syncing spread and on 15 November 1990 Farian himself announced that Morvan and Pilatus had not sung. The Grammy was withdrawn four days later and Arista removed the album from its catalogue, making it the best-selling album ever to be taken off the market.

After that the duo continued in the 1990s as Rob & Fab, with limited success. Morvan returned in the 2000s with the solo album Love Revolution in 2003. His name stands for one of the greatest scandals in pop history and for the question of what authenticity in pop music means.
artiest/fab-morvan.listen: Listen to Girl You Know It's True or Blame It on the Rain and notice the polished production, with danceable beat, strong vocal melody and rap, which was then presented as the voice of Milli Vanilli.

artiest/fabio-pignatelli.text:
Fabio Pignatelli is an Italian musician and the bass guitarist of the Italian progressive rock band Goblin. That group made the music for several horror films, best known for Dario Argento's Suspiria from 1977 and George A. Romero's Dawn of the Dead from 1978. By 1983 the band had largely broken up, but Pignatelli held the group together and continued to use the name. In this way it carried on until the end of the 1980s, and in 2000 the main line-up briefly came together again.

For the film Tenebrae, with the soundtrack Tenebre from 1982, the band was credited as Simonetti-Pignatelli-Morante. The other members, among them Maurizio Guarini and Carlo Pennisi, were not involved in it, and because Pignatelli controlled the group name, that wording was chosen. In 2013 he played bass guitar on the track Backlit from the album Simulakrum Lab, a project with vintage synthesizers by Paolo Prevosto.

Pignatelli is part of the Italian tradition in which progressive rock and film music come together. The bass lines form the solid ground for the synthesizers and guitars, and helped to create a cold, menacing sound that suits horror. Goblin showed how strongly music can carry a film and thereby became a model for later film composers in the genre.
artiest/fabio-pignatelli.listen: Listen to Goblin's music for Suspiria and notice the menacing, constantly recurring bass line and the synthesizer sounds that together build an oppressive atmosphere.

artiest/fairuz.text: Fairuz, born Nouhad Haddad in Beirut, began as a choir singer on Lebanese radio. There she met the brothers Assi and Mansour Rahbani, who from her first hit Itab (1952) wrote almost all her songs: short, clear songs instead of hours-long Egyptian performances. From 1957 she performed at the Baalbek festival, and in 1961 she also recorded songs by Mohammed Abdel Wahab. Many Arab radio stations still open the morning with her voice.
artiest/fairuz.listen: Listen to Sakana al leyel, a song by Abdel Wahab, and hear how clearly and restrainedly Fairuz sings, without the long ornaments of Oum Kalthoum.

artiest/faith-no-more.text:
Faith No More is an American rock group from San Francisco. The foundations were laid around 1979, when the drummer Mike Bordin, the bassist Billy Gould and others played under names such as Sharp Young Men and Faith. No Man. After Bordin, Gould and the keyboard player Roddy Bottum left that group, they continued as Faith No More. With the singer Chuck Mosley and the guitarist Jim Martin, the albums We Care a Lot (1985) and Introduce Yourself (1987) appeared.

In 1988 the singer Mike Patton joined the band. With him Faith No More broke through with The Real Thing in 1989. The single Epic reached the American top ten and received heavy airplay on MTV. Angel Dust (1992), King for a Day… Fool for a Lifetime (1995) and Album of the Year (1997) followed. In 1998 the group stopped, in 2009 it came back, and in 2015 Sol Invictus appeared.

The music combines funk, metal, hip hop, pop melodies and progressive rock. Patton switches effortlessly from rap to singing, and the band dared to be experimental even on a major label, especially on Angel Dust. Faith No More is regarded as a forerunner of the funk rock and alternative metal of the 1990s. In a single song, Epic shows how rap, funk and guitar rock can come together.
artiest/faith-no-more.listen: Listen to Epic and notice the transition between the rap-like verses and the heavy, melodic chorus. Can you hear how bass guitar and guitar then shift from funk to metal?

artiest/falco.text:
Falco's real name was Johann Hölzel and he was born in 1957 in a working-class district of Vienna. He wanted to be a pop star from an early age, but did not last long at the conservatoire. In the late 1970s he played bass in the Viennese underground scene, including in the punk group Drahdiwaberl. He borrowed his stage name from the East German ski jumper Falko Weißpflog. With short hair, suits and sunglasses he looked sleeker than the rest of that scene.

In 1981 he went solo, with the songwriter Robert Ponger. Der Kommissar was actually intended as a B-side, but his manager thought it stronger than the planned single. The song is about drug use and combines rapped verses in German with a sung chorus. Rap was still rare in Western Europe at the time. Der Kommissar became a number 1 in, among other countries, Germany, France, Italy and Japan, and the album Einzelhaft also topped the chart in the Netherlands. After the less successful Junge Roemer (1984), Falco began working with the Dutch producers Rob and Ferdi Bolland. This produced Rock Me Amadeus, which reached number 1 in the United States in 1986: the only German-language song ever to do so. Vienna Calling and Jeanny also became hits.

Falco struggled with alcohol and cocaine, and a lasting career in America never materialised. In 1998, at the age of 40, he died in a road accident in the Dominican Republic. In the United States he is sometimes called the father of white rap.
artiest/falco.listen: Listen to Der Kommissar and notice the difference between the verses, which Falco half speaks and half raps in German, and the sung chorus. Hear too how the tight bass line and the electronic sounds carry the song.

artiest/famoudou-don-moye.text:
Famoudou Don Moye, born Donald Moye Jr. in 1946 in Rochester, New York, is an American jazz drummer and percussionist. As a boy he played in drum and bugle corps and in a church choir, and was given violin lessons. He came into contact with jazz young: his mother worked for a social club with a jazz club next door, where Kenny Burrell and Jimmy McGriff, among others, performed. His father played drums. Moye studied percussion at Wayne State University in Detroit, where the trumpeter Charles Moore became his mentor. He played in the African Cultural Ensemble and in Moore's band Detroit Free Jazz. In 1968 he went to Europe with that band and stayed there for a few years, travelling through Europe and North Africa.

In Paris he practised at the American Center for Students and Artists. There Roscoe Mitchell asked him to join the Art Ensemble of Chicago, which consisted of Mitchell, Joseph Jarman, Lester Bowie and Malachi Favors Maghostut and had as yet no regular drummer. Moye became a core member. He is best known for his mastery of African and Caribbean percussion instruments and rhythmic techniques. Under his own name he released, among others, Sun Percussion, Volume One in 1975, Black Paladins in 1980, Afrikan Song in 1996 and Ancestral Memories: From Afrika to Chicago in 1998.

With the Art Ensemble, Moye brought a broad palette of percussion sounds into avant-garde jazz. Instead of a fixed beat he added colours, rhythms from Africa and the Caribbean and a large arsenal of small instruments. In this way he belongs to the AACM tradition that reconnected jazz with its African roots.
artiest/famoudou-don-moye.listen: Listen to a recording of the Art Ensemble of Chicago with Moye and notice the many different percussion and sound instruments, such as drums, bells and small percussion, which together create an atmosphere of their own.

artiest/fanfare-ciocarlia.text:
Fanfare Ciocărlia is a Roma brass band from Zece Prăjini, a village in north-eastern Romania inhabited exclusively by Roma families. There making music is a family tradition. The men work as farmers or in a nearby factory and play at weddings and christening parties. In 1996 the German sound engineer Henry Ernst travelled to the region to look for village musicians. There he found a brass band led by the clarinettist Ioan Ivancea.

Ernst and his colleague Neumann recorded the group in Bucharest in 1997. The debut album Radio Pașcani appeared in 1998 on the Berlin label Piranha Musik and was an instant hit. Baro Biao in 1999 and Iag Bari in 2001 followed, and the group toured Europe, the United States, Japan and Australia. Later came, among others, Gili Garabdi in 2005 and Balkan Brass Battle in 2011, an album on which the band took on a Serbian brass band. In 2012 it played at the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony in Oslo.

The sound consists of trumpets, tubas, clarinets, saxophones and percussion. The music is lightning-fast and has complex rhythms, with staccato solos from the brass. The sources are Roma and Romanian folk dances, supplemented with Turkish, Bulgarian and Serbian influences. Fanfare Ciocărlia brought Balkan brass to clubs and festivals, to an audience that appreciated rock, rave and world music alike.
artiest/fanfare-ciocarlia.listen: Listen to Iag Bari and follow how fast the trumpets and clarinets play their solos while tuba and percussion hold the tempo. Can you hear what a wedding dance pattern is?

artiest/fanny-mendelssohn.text: Fanny Mendelssohn was as gifted a pianist and composer as her brother Felix, but her family did not consider a public career suitable for a woman. In the parental home in Berlin she led the Sonntagsmusiken, where her own work was played, and some of her songs were published under Felix's name. Her piano cycle Das Jahr from 1841 gives each month a piece of its own. Only in 1846, shortly before her death, did she publish under her own name.
artiest/fanny-mendelssohn.listen: Listen to January from Das Jahr and hear how the piece begins like a dream, with floating chords that seem to have no fixed metre.

artiest/farley-jackmaster-funk.text:
Farley Jackmaster Funk, born Farley Keith Williams in 1962, is an American DJ, musician and producer from Chicago, a pioneer of house and acid house. In the mid and late 1980s he wrote and produced several influential tracks. Under other names he appeared as Farley Funkin' Keith, The Housemaster Boyz and The Godfather of House. In 1981 he was one of the original members of the Hot Mix 5, a DJ team on the radio station WBMX in Oak Park, Illinois. He played as a guest at the Warehouse and as a regular at The Playground.

In 1985 he started the label House Records with Chip E., with Jack Trax as its first release. His own debut single was Aw Shucks (Let's Go Let's Go), followed by Funkin with the Drums, with bare beat tracks of drums alone. His single Jack the Bass kicked off the jacking craze in Chicago in 1985. Give Yourself to Me followed. In 1986, with Jesse Saunders, he made a version of his own of the cover of I Can't Turn Around by Isaac Hayes that his housemate Steve Silk Hurley had produced. Vince Lawrence's new lyrics changed the hook to Love Can't Turn Around, sung by Darryl Pandy. The song reached number ten on the British chart and was the first house hit there.

With that Farley brought house across the ocean. His music consists of solid drum machines, bass and short vocal hooks, made for the dance floor. His album No Vocals Necessary appeared in 1988. He belongs to the makers who made Chicago the cradle of house.
artiest/farley-jackmaster-funk.listen: Listen to Love Can't Turn Around and notice the tight drum machine and bass line, and how Darryl Pandy's vocals rise above the electronic beat.

artiest/fatboy-slim.text:
Fatboy Slim is the artist alias of Norman Cook, an English musician and DJ who was born Quentin Cook in Bromley in 1963. He began in punk, played bass with the Housemartins in the 1980s and in 1986 had a British number one with Caravan of Love. After the end of that band he moved to Brighton to make dance music. There he formed Beats International, with the number one Dub Be Good to Me in 1990, and later Freak Power.

Cook adopted the name Fatboy Slim in 1995. In Brighton he started the club night Big Beat Boutique, where he mixed breakbeats with northern soul, acid house, hip hop and reggae. The big beat genre takes its name from that night. His first album Better Living Through Chemistry appeared in 1996. The second, You've Come a Long Way, Baby from 1998, contained The Rockafeller Skank, Praise You and Right Here, Right Now. Halfway Between the Gutter and the Stars followed in 2000.

The music leans heavily on samples from all kinds of genres, combined with pop structures, processed rhythms and short, slogan-like vocals. Fatboy Slim showed that a DJ with a sampler and a solid beat could conquer the charts, and made the DJ a pop star on festival stages. In this way he belongs to the wave of DJs who brought dance to a large audience in the 1990s.
artiest/fatboy-slim.listen: Listen to The Rockafeller Skank and notice how a short spoken phrase and a guitar sample keep coming back over a hard breakbeat. Can you hear how little material the song needs to keep going?

artiest/fats-domino.text:
Fats Domino's full name was Antoine Caliste Domino and he was born in New Orleans in 1928, into a French-speaking Creole family. Around the age of ten he learned to play the piano from his brother-in-law, a jazz guitarist. At fourteen he was already playing in the bars of the city. Bandleader Billy Diamond heard him at a barbecue in 1947, took him into his band and gave him the nickname Fats.

In 1949 he signed with Imperial Records. With the producer and trumpeter Dave Bartholomew he wrote The Fat Man, a polished version of an old blues song. With its rolling piano, Domino's humming wah-wah and a solid backbeat, some historians regard it as the first rock 'n' roll single. A million copies were sold. Domino also played piano on Lawdy Miss Clawdy by Lloyd Price (1952). From Ain't That a Shame (1955) a long run of hits followed, including Blueberry Hill and Walking to New Orleans. His band, with saxophonists such as Herbert Hardesty and Lee Allen and the drummer Earl Palmer, gave the records their warm, relaxed New Orleans sound.

Domino was shy and modest, but his influence was great. Elvis Presley called him the real king of rock 'n' roll, and The Beatles too learned from him. In 1986 he was among the very first group of artists in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. He died in 2017.
artiest/fats-domino.listen: Listen to The Fat Man and notice Domino's left hand on the piano, which keeps repeating a rolling pattern. Hear how he sings wah-wah above it, and how the drums hit firmly on the second and fourth beats.

artiest/fats-navarro.text:
Theodore Fats Navarro was an American jazz trumpeter and a pioneer of bebop in the 1940s. He was born in Key West, Florida, in 1923, with Cuban, African and Chinese ancestors, and spoke Spanish as well as English. His father, a barber, had him take piano lessons as a child. He began playing piano at six and trumpet at thirteen. He was also so good on tenor saxophone that in his first years he played both professionally. In 1941 he moved north and played in the band of Sol Allbright.

In the Midwest he played with Snookum Russell, where he influenced the young J.J. Johnson, and then in the big bands of Andy Kirk, Benny Goodman and Lionel Hampton. Billy Eckstine took him into his band, which was full of young bebop musicians. He made his last recordings with Kirk and Eckstine in 1946. After that he became famous as a bebopper in New York, with studio sessions with Tadd Dameron, Bud Powell and Kenny Clarke. He fell ill with tuberculosis and died in 1950, at the age of twenty-six.

His career was short, but his influence was great. Trumpeters such as Miles Davis, Clifford Brown and Lee Morgan adopted his style. His playing was known for its full tone and long, flowing improvised lines. Records such as The Fabulous Fats Navarro, Volume 1 and Fats Navarro Memorial Album preserve his work. He shows how bebop could sound on the trumpet without speed coming at the expense of beauty.
artiest/fats-navarro.listen: Listen to Our Delight and notice the clear trumpet tone and how Navarro plays long, fast lines that nevertheless remain melodic.

artiest/fats-waller.text: Thomas 'Fats' Waller was the son of a minister in Harlem and as a boy played the organ in church. He became a pupil of James P. Johnson and developed a light, swinging stride style. With the lyricist Andy Razaf he wrote songs such as Ain't Misbehavin' and Honeysuckle Rose. From 1934 he recorded hundreds of records with his small group Fats Waller and His Rhythm, often with funny comments between the lines. That made him a popular entertainer on radio and in films. Behind the jokes was a strong pianist and organist. He died in 1943 of pneumonia on a train, on the way from Los Angeles to New York.
artiest/fats-waller.listen: Hear how light and playful the stride sounds: virtuosic, but effortless.

artiest/fats-waller-and-his-rhythm.text:
Fats Waller and His Rhythm was the name under which the pianist Fats Waller made records with a small group. Thomas Wright Fats Waller was born in New York in 1904, the seventh of eleven children, of whom five survived childhood. His father was a Baptist lay preacher and his mother was a musician. He began piano at the age of six, played the harmonium at his father's open-air services and also learned double bass and violin. He played well by ear. He got the nickname Fats as a boy, because of his weight. He grew up in Harlem, under the influence of the Harlem Renaissance.

Waller was a pianist, organist, composer and singer. He was an innovator of the stride style and became a popular performer in the Jazz Age and the swing era, with tours of the United States and Europe. His best-known songs, Ain't Misbehavin' and Honeysuckle Rose, are in the Grammy Hall of Fame. He wrote hundreds of songs, often without credit, because he sold the rights for ready cash. He played with witty asides and facial expressions, which worked well on the radio and in the clubs. Towards the end of his life he wanted the public to take jazz as seriously as classical music.

His recordings number hundreds of titles. He combines virtuoso stride piano with humour and showed that serious technique and entertainment do not exclude one another. He died in 1943. Anyone who wants to hear how jazz sounded in the 1930s will find in his records a clear, spirited yardstick.
artiest/fats-waller-and-his-rhythm.listen: Listen to Ain't Misbehavin' and notice the firm left hand of the stride piano and the playful, almost talking way in which Waller sings.

artiest/feist.text:
Leslie Feist, known as Feist, is a Canadian indie pop singer and songwriter, born in Amherst, Nova Scotia, in 1976. Her parents were both artists: her father was an abstract expressionist painter, her mother studied ceramics. After their divorce she moved with her mother and brother to Regina and later to Calgary. She wanted to be a writer and sang a lot in choirs. At the age of twelve she danced in the opening ceremony of the Winter Olympics in Calgary, which later inspired the video for 1234. In 1991, at fifteen, she founded the punk band Placebo in Calgary, of which she was the singer.

Her solo career began in 1999 with Monarch: Lay Your Jewelled Head Down. She also plays in the indie rock group Broken Social Scene. The records Let It Die from 2004 and The Reminder from 2007 were acclaimed and together sold more than two and a half million copies. The Reminder earned four Grammy nominations, including for best new artist. Metals in 2011, Pleasure in 2017 and Multitudes in 2023 followed. In 2012 she made a split EP with the metal group Mastodon. She won eleven Juno Awards, including two for artist of the year.

Feist's music is intimate and acoustic, with a warm, sometimes raw voice, and a preference for simple instrumentation. In this way she belongs to the Canadian indie wave of the beginning of this century and showed that a singer-songwriter could exist both in the indie scene and in the big charts.
artiest/feist.listen: Listen to 1234 from The Reminder and notice how the song is slowly built up, from a simple beginning to a full, festive chorus with harmony vocals.

artiest/fejat-sejdic.text:
Fejat Sejdić was a Serbian Roma trumpeter and leader of a brass band from Bojnik in southern Serbia. He was born on 20 January 1941 and died on 22 August 2017. His father and grandfather also played the trumpet. Fejat learned it as a child by ear, on the family's only trumpet, and at ten he already played like an adult. He never learned to read music.

He became known at the Guča Trumpet Festival, the largest trumpet festival in the world. His orchestra won the prize for best orchestra there a record six times, between 1976 and 1994, and he also received the prize for best trumpeter and the Golden Trumpet. After that he played only as a guest. He performed in major cities in Europe and beyond, contributed to film music by Goran Bregović and Živojin Pavlović and played with the Gipsy Kings. His discography numbers some sixty records. A stroke in 2001 meant he could no longer play. His grandson Nebojša later continued the orchestra.

His sound was so recognisable that people said you could pick him out among twenty orchestras. He set a high standard in the Balkan brass world, and after his breakthrough the number of orchestras in Bojnik grew from one to fifteen. Fejat Sejdić belongs to the Roma tradition that also returns in the course as a source of Balkan music.
artiest/fejat-sejdic.listen: Listen to Kondorov let and focus on the trumpet: how high and clear is the tone, and how much ornamentation does he play into the melody? Listen too to what the orchestra does underneath.

artiest/fela-kuti.text:
Fela Kuti, born Olufela Olusegun Oludotun Ransome-Kuti in 1938 in Abeokuta, Nigeria, was a musician and political activist and is regarded as the most important innovator of afrobeat, a style that combines West African music with American funk and jazz. He came from a well-off family. His mother Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti was an anti-colonial feminist, his father an Anglican minister and headmaster. His cousin was the writer Wole Soyinka. In 1958 he went to London to study at Trinity College of Music, with the trumpet as his instrument.

In the 1970s, with his band Africa '70, with the drummer and musical director Tony Allen, he became a star in Nigeria. He was an outspoken critic of the military regimes and also became their target. In 1970 he founded the Kalakuta Republic, a commune that declared itself independent of military rule. In 1977 it was destroyed by the army, in which Kuti was injured and his mother was killed. In 1984 the Buhari government imprisoned him, and he was released after twenty months. His records from those years include Shakara, Gentleman, Zombie and Kalakuta Show, often with long tracks of more than ten minutes. After his death in 1997, his son Femi Kuti oversaw reissues.

Kuti's music is built on a continuous rhythmic groove, with sharp brass, high vocal choruses and long improvisations, and with lyrics about power and injustice in Nigeria. He showed that pop music could be a political weapon. In 2026 he was posthumously inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/fela-kuti.listen: Listen to Zombie and notice how the rhythm, the horns and the answering chorus are repeated again and again and together form a long, compelling groove.

artiest/fela-kuti-en-africa-70.text:
Fela Kuti was born Olufela Ransome-Kuti in 1938 in Abeokuta, Nigeria, into a family that resisted colonialism. His mother Funmilayo was a feminist who in 1946 led the Abeokuta women's revolt. His cousin was the writer Wole Soyinka. Fela went to London in 1958 to study music. Later, with his band Africa 70, he formed a group of which the drummer Tony Allen was the musical director. In the 1970s the band grew into a star in Nigeria.

Kuti is regarded as the founder of Afrobeat, a style that combines West African music with American funk and jazz. In 1970 he founded the commune Kalakuta Republic, which declared itself independent of military rule. In 1977 the army destroyed the commune, in which Fela was injured and his mother was killed. In 1984 the government of Muhammadu Buhari imprisoned him, until his release after twenty months. He continued to record and perform until his death in 1997. His son Femi Kuti now oversees the reissues of his music. In 2026 Fela was posthumously inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

The songs are long, with rhythms that repeat, horns, singing in an alternation of leader and chorus and lyrics that attack authority. Zombie from 1976 is about soldiers who obey orders without thinking, and Water No Get Enemy from 1975 about water as a life force. Fela showed that dance music could at the same time be a political weapon.
artiest/fela-kuti-en-africa-70.listen: Listen to Zombie and notice the repeating rhythms, the horns and the alternation between the singer and the chorus. Hear how the music almost never stops and keeps carrying you along.
